findings.issue_text: [BUG] parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the full safeParse result object ({success, data}), and GoogleCalendarService stores that wrapper directly as credential.key instead of the parsed token data that the removed googleCredentialSchema.parse returned. On the first token refresh after this deploys — even with credential sharing disabled — every Google credential's key becomes {success:true, data:{...}}, so the next googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key) throws and all Google Calendar booking/availability operations fail until each user re-connects the integration.

[BUG] appStoreMetadata is an array of per-app metadata objects (consumed elsewhere via .find(app => app.slug === ...)), so appStoreMetadata[app.slug as keyof typeof appStoreMetadata] indexes that array with a slug string and evaluates to undefined for every app. The app-credential webhook returns 404 'App not found. Ensure that you have the correct app slug' for every valid app slug, so the credential-sync feature this PR adds never successfully processes a single request on any deployment that enables it.

[BUG] In sharing mode refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response from CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT (never calling .json()), while every consumer expects the provider-shaped token object it previously received (axios .data, GaxiosResponse .data, or typed token fields). With credential sharing enabled, Google's refresh crashes reading token.access_token of undefined (res?.data on a Response), zoho-bigin and zohocrm crash reading tokenInfo.data.error of undefined, and HubSpot computes a NaN expiry from undefined token fields and persists it, so token refresh is broken for those apps.

[BUG] The computed keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] both evaluate to the literal string '[object Object]' (zod schemas use Object.prototype.toString and the duplicate object-literal key collapses to the second value), so the intended 'any property with a number is the expiry' check does not exist and the schema degenerates to z.object({access_token: z.string(), '[object Object]': z.unknown().optional()}). In sharing mode the parse validates only access_token and strips every other property (expiry_date, instance_url, scope) via z.object's default strip behavior, then parseRefreshTokenResponse writes refresh_token:'refresh_token' into the output, so consumers persist credentials with no expiry data and a garbage refresh_token placeholder.

[BUG] SalesforceCalendarService now unconditionally performs an eager POST to login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token plus a prisma.credential.update on every instantiation, ungated by APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED, unlike every other app in this diff which wraps its existing lazy refresh inside refreshOAuthTokens. Every Salesforce calendar operation now pays an extra Salesforce OAuth round-trip and a credential DB write per instantiation, and any transient Salesforce non-200 (rate limit, blip, or expired refresh token) throws HttpError from the response.statusText !== 'OK' check during construction, failing bookings that previously succeeded using the still-valid stored access token; the statusText check also discards the error body.

[BUG] zoho-bigin passes credentialId — the credential's string identifier — as refreshOAuthTokens's userId: number | null parameter, where every sibling call site in this diff passes credential.userId. The call fails typecheck (string not assignable to number | null) and breaks the app-store build, or, if credentialId resolves to some in-scope local, it ships a credential id as calcomUserId to the sync endpoint, which returns tokens for the wrong entity and silently cross-links credentials.

[ADVISORY] The outbound POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT carries no authentication of any kind — no secret header — even though the inbound direction of the same feature is protected by CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET. Anyone who can reach the operator's sync endpoint can POST sequential calcomUserId values and harvest live OAuth access tokens for every user, making the endpoint an unauthenticated credential oracle while Cal.com's side of the same integration insists on a shared secret.

[ADVISORY] The stated prerequisite '# must be 32 bytes for AES256 encryption algorithm' is contradicted by the recommended command 'openssl rand -base64 24', which generates 24 random bytes (a 32-character base64 string), not a 32-byte key. A self-hoster who follows the 32-byte requirement (openssl rand -base64 32, producing a 44-character value) or whose crypto layer base64-decodes the configured value supplies an invalid AES-256 key length, and every symmetricDecrypt call in the app-credential webhook throws; the two instructions cannot both be correct, so integrators must guess which one the implementation honors.

[ADVISORY] The handler validates with appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse and JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) with no try/catch or defaultResponder error envelope, so every malformed input propagates as an unhandled throw. The parent application integrating with this webhook receives bare 500s (Next's default error handling) with no actionable message for wrong-shaped bodies, undecryptable ciphertext, or wrong HTTP methods — the exact operator this feature targets cannot debug their first sync payload without server log access.

[ADVISORY] The webhook secret is compared with !== instead of crypto.timingSafeEqual, and this comparison is the sole authentication for an endpoint that writes OAuth credentials for arbitrary body-supplied userIds. An attacker positioned on the same network as a self-hosted instance (the low-jitter environment this feature targets) gets a first-mismatch timing oracle on the shared secret and can then overwrite any user's app credentials once it is recovered.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds a credential-writing API controller and two shared OAuth utilities consumed by ten apps with zero tests — nothing exercises the webhook's auth/decrypt/upsert paths or the sharing-mode branches of refreshOAuthTokens and parseRefreshTokenResponse. Every defect in the new code ships undetected because no test in the diff executes it — the wrapper-persistence and raw-Response bugs above would each have been caught by a single refresh-flow test, and the first production regression in the sharing path breaks connected apps' token refresh with no pinned behavior to detect it.

[BUG] Google's token refresh stores the zod safeParse wrapper returned by parseRefreshTokenResponse directly as the credential key (data: { key }), because parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the full SafeParseReturnType while the code it replaced, googleCredentialSchema.parse, returned the parsed object itself. On the first access-token refresh after deploying this change (no feature flags required, sharing disabled), prisma.credential.update persists key = {success: true, data: {...}}, so every later Google Calendar operation reads credential.key.access_token and .refresh_token as undefined, the next refreshToken call fails with invalid_grant, and all Google Calendar bookings error until each user manually reconnects — silent, unrecoverable destruction of stored OAuth tokens on the standard path.

[BUG] parseRefreshTokenResponse unconditionally injects the literal string 'refresh_token' into the parsed data whenever the provider's refresh response omits a refresh token — the normal case for Microsoft's refresh grant and the case Zoom's own code documents as recurring (VideoApiAdapter.ts TODO referencing refresh token not always being returned) — and callers spread this mutated data into the stored credential key. Any Office365 or Zoom token refresh whose response omits refresh_token (previously handled by falling back to the old token) persists the string 'refresh_token' as the user's real refresh token, so the next refresh sends the literal to the provider, gets invalid_grant, and the integration is bricked until re-authorization — with sharing disabled, on the standard path.

[BUG] Office365's refresh now runs through parseRefreshTokenResponse, which either throws on schema failure (where the removed code logged console.error and spread nothing, keeping the old credentials intact) or, when Microsoft's refresh response omits refresh_token, has the literal 'refresh_token' injected into tokenResponse.data, which this spread then writes over the real stored refresh token before prisma.credential.update persists it. Every Office365 token refresh after this deploy either fails loudly (booking breaks, the old soft-failure fallback is gone) or silently replaces the user's valid refresh token with the string 'refresh_token', after which all refreshes return invalid_grant and the user must reconnect Office365 — no error is surfaced at write time.

[BUG] Both computed keys in minimumTokenResponseSchema — [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] — stringify to the identical '[object Object]' (zod schemas do not override Object.prototype.toString), so the second duplicate key silently replaces the first, the commented 'any property with a number is the expiry' rule is never expressed, and in zod's default strip mode the schema validates only access_token and deletes every other property from the parsed data. With sharing enabled, every refresh parse strips refresh_token, expiry_date, instance_url, token_type and scope from the data callers persist: google's token.expiry_date is never populated, salesforce's stored key loses instance_url, and stored credentials no longer satisfy the app schemas the rest of the code parses them with — the feature's own stated acceptance criterion (accept an expiry under any key name) is not implemented at all.

[BUG] In sharing mode refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw fetch Response from the operator's CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, but every call site was written for the provider-specific shape it replaced (gaxios res with .data, axios response with .data, hubspot token object), and no caller ever calls response.json() on the sync response. With sharing enabled, googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:93-94 throws TypeError reading 'access_token' of undefined (res?.data on a fetch Response), zoho-bigin CalendarService.ts:96 and zohocrm CalendarService.ts:217 throw TypeError reading 'error' of undefined (tokenInfo.data), and hubspot CalendarService.ts:176 consumes the Response as a HubspotToken whose fields are all undefined and persists it — the credential-sync feature crashes or corrupts on every adapter it was wired into.

[BUG] parseRefreshTokenResponse's mode check omits the '&& userId' condition its sibling refreshOAuthTokens applies, so team-owned credentials (userId null, e.g. Zoom/Hubspot installed on a team via createOAuthAppCredential) are refreshed directly against the provider but still parsed with minimumTokenResponseSchema. With the sharing flags on, a team credential's real provider refresh response is stripped to {access_token} and the literal 'refresh_token' injected, so the stored team credential loses its real refresh_token and expiry fields even though the sync path was never used for it — org-level integrations break the moment an operator enables the feature.

[BUG] zoho-bigin passes 'credentialId' (the credential row id) as the userId argument where every sibling adapter passes credential.userId, so refreshOAuthTokens' sync branch posts that credential id as calcomUserId. With sharing enabled, the parent application receives a credential id where its contract expects a cal.com user id, resolves the wrong user (ids numerically overlap between the tables) or none, and Zoho Bigin credential sync updates the wrong account's data or fails for every Bigin user.

[BUG] Salesforce refreshes directly against login.salesforce.com but its parse honors the sharing flags, so with sharing enabled the full valid Salesforce response is stripped by minimumTokenResponseSchema to {access_token} before prisma.credential.update persists { ...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token } — and the 'if (!accessTokenParsed.success)' guard at line 92 is dead code because parseRefreshTokenResponse already throws on failure. The stored Salesforce credential loses instance_url, id, issued_at, signature, scope and token_type that the callback-stored key contained, so the jsforce.Connection built next and any later read of credential.key.instance_url operates on a degraded key and Salesforce calendar operations fail — while the author's error branch never executes, hiding the divergence.

[BUG] parseRefreshTokenResponse breaks the contract stated by the adjacent code: it throws 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' when zoomRefreshedTokenSchema fails — while the TODO two lines below requires that an invalid token 'initiate the fallback sequence instead of throwing' — and on the omission path it injects the literal 'refresh_token' into the data, while in sharing mode it skips zoomRefreshedTokenSchema entirely. A Zoom refresh response that omits refresh_token (the recurring case this code documents) either throws and kills the booking instead of falling back to the old token, or hands the downstream refresh_token-fallback a truthy literal that overwrites the real token; in sharing mode the structure check the comment promises is silently disabled, so malformed sync responses get persisted as credentials.

[BUG] The upsert targets findFirst({ userId, appId }) and updates whichever credential row Prisma returns first, but cal.com supports multiple credentials per user per app (e.g. two Google accounts referenced by different event types), so the sync has no way to address a specific credential. A credential push intended for a user's second account of an app silently overwrites the first account's stored token with the wrong keys, and the create branch is unreachable for any user who already holds one credential of that app — bookings attached to the overwritten credential then authenticate as the wrong OAuth account.

[BUG] The handler has no HTTP method guard and no error handling: appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body) throws an unhandled ZodError for a missing or malformed body and for a string userId (e.g. "3"), and symmetricDecrypt/JSON.parse failures at lines 57-59 throw unhandled as well. An integrating parent application sending a GET, a non-JSON body, a string userId, or wrongly encrypted keys receives an unhandled 500 with no 4xx/5xx distinction and no diagnostic body, so every client-side integration mistake becomes an opaque server error that must be debugged from server logs instead of a contract-violation response.

[ADVISORY] The diff ships three new behavior-bearing modules — the app-credential webhook route, parseRefreshTokenResponse, and refreshOAuthTokens, which together control credential persistence for roughly ten adapters — with zero test files anywhere in the diff (no spec/**, test/**, *.test.*, or *.spec.* paths appear). The Google safeParse-wrapper corruption (googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:96 persisting {success, data} as the credential key) shipped through exactly this gap — any single assertion on the persisted key shape or on parseRefreshTokenResponse's return value would have caught it — and the same silence now covers the webhook's auth/upsert logic and the sharing-mode branch of every adapter.

[ADVISORY] The Salesforce service now performs an eager token refresh — a POST to login.salesforce.com plus a prisma.credential.update — on every SalesforceCalendarService construction, where the pre-diff jsforce.Connection refreshed lazily on token expiry. Every booking and calendar operation touching Salesforce pays a serial network round trip and a credential-row DB write on the hot path, Salesforce's token endpoint sees refresh-grant volume multiplied by operation count (rate-limit exposure), and concurrent constructions race last-write-wins on the credential key.

[ADVISORY] The webhook persists the decrypted 'keys' blob to credential.key with no per-app schema validation, even though every other credential-write path in the apps this diff touches zod-parses keys (googleCredentialSchema, refreshTokenResponseSchema, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema). A parent application whose payload drifts from the expected app-key shape receives a 200 'Credentials updated' and silently poisons the user's stored credential, which then fails at runtime with schema errors far from the write — the operator gets no 4xx signal at sync time to catch the drift.

[ADVISORY] The outbound sync request to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only calcomUserId and appSlug with no auth header and no extension point to add one, while the inbound direction of this same feature is guarded by a shared secret and header check. The operator's sync endpoint must return live OAuth access tokens to any unauthenticated caller who posts a userId and appSlug, or the operator must fork this helper to attach credentials — the feature's security model is asymmetric between its two directions, with no flag, option, or documentation covering the outbound side.

[ADVISORY] CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME is used verbatim as the header lookup key, but Node lowercases all incoming request headers, so any uppercase character in the configured name makes the lookup miss — the only guard is a 'Should be in lowercase' comment in .env.example, with no .toLowerCase() normalization or startup validation. An operator who sets CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME='Calcom-Webhook-Secret' gets a silent permanent 403 'Invalid webhook secret' on every credential push despite sending the correct secret, and nothing in logs or config validation points at the case mismatch.

[ADVISORY] The webhook secret is verified with plain !== string equality on an unauthenticated route that writes credentials for arbitrary userIds, instead of a constant-time comparison (crypto.timingSafeEqual). An attacker who can reach the endpoint and measure response timing gets a byte-by-byte oracle on the shared secret; because possession of that single secret authorizes overwriting any user's app credentials, the route's only authentication layer rests on a non-constant-time comparison.

[BUG] parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the zod safeParse envelope ({success, data}) rather than the parsed data, and GoogleCalendarService persists that envelope directly as the credential key via data: { key }. On the default (non-sync) configuration every Google token refresh writes {success:true, data:{...}} into Credential.key, so the next read of credential.key.refresh_token/access_token is undefined — Google Calendar breaks for every user within one access-token lifetime and each corrupted credential requires user re-authentication.

[BUG] In credential-sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response, but the Google code reads res?.data and then dereferences token.access_token, which is undefined on a Response. With credential sync enabled, every Google token refresh throws TypeError (reading 'access_token' of undefined) before any token is persisted, so Google Calendar is unusable in the very mode this PR introduces, regardless of what the sync endpoint returns.

[BUG] When the parsed response lacks refresh_token the code overwrites it with the literal placeholder string 'refresh_token' instead of preserving the caller's existing token, and call sites persist that placeholder over the real secret (Office365CalendarService line 263 spreads tokenResponse.data over o365AuthCredentials before its credential.update; Zoom stores parsedToken.data). With credential sync enabled, the first O365/Zoom token refresh replaces the user's real stored refresh token with the string 'refresh_token' (and zod's strip behavior also drops the expiry field), permanently destroying the credential — it stays broken even after sync is later disabled — and forcing re-authentication.

[BUG] In sync mode tokenInfo is a fetch Response, but the code reads tokenInfo.data.error, and a fetch Response has no data property. With sync enabled every zoho-bigin refresh throws TypeError reading 'error' of undefined, so Bigin integration fails in the feature's primary mode regardless of the sync endpoint's payload.

[BUG] In sync mode zohoCrmTokenInfo is a fetch Response but is consumed as an axios response via zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error. With sync enabled every zohocrm refresh throws TypeError reading 'error' of undefined, breaking Zoho CRM in the feature's primary mode.

[BUG] The outbound credential-sync request sends only calcomUserId and appSlug with no authentication of any kind — no header, no signature, no CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET — even though the inbound webhook enforces a shared secret. Anyone who learns the CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT URL can POST arbitrary userId/appSlug pairs and receive live OAuth access tokens for any user (full credential theft), and a legitimate parent app has no client credential to verify the request with since none is sent.

[BUG] zoho-bigin passes credentialId (the credential row identifier) as refreshOAuthTokens' userId parameter, unlike every sibling call site which passes credential.userId. With sync enabled the credential-sync endpoint receives calcomUserId=<credential id>, maps it to a nonexistent or wrong parent-app user, and zoho-bigin token sync returns wrong or no tokens for every Bigin user.

[BUG] In sync mode hubspotRefreshToken is a raw fetch Response but is consumed as a HubspotToken, so .refresh_token and .expires_in are undefined. With sync enabled the first Hubspot refresh persists a credential whose refresh_token is undefined and whose expiry computes to NaN, destroying the stored credential and putting Hubspot into a permanent refresh/auth failure loop.

[BUG] Both computed property keys — [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] — evaluate to the same literal string '[object Object]' (zod schemas do not override toString), so the second entry overwrites the first and the 'any property with a number is the expiry' validation the comment promises does not exist. minimumTokenResponseSchema enforces only access_token, so sync responses with missing or malformed expiry fields pass validation; callers then persist credentials whose expiry never advances and re-enter the refresh path on every call.

[BUG] A new unconditional Salesforce token refresh (direct fetch to login.salesforce.com plus a credential DB write) runs on every SalesforceCalendarService instantiation, gated on neither token expiry nor the credential-sync configuration, and it bypasses refreshOAuthTokens entirely. Every Salesforce calendar operation now pays an extra Salesforce round-trip and a DB write (latency and API rate-limit exposure), and with credential sharing enabled Salesforce still refreshes directly against Salesforce, violating the feature's own invariant that enabled sync routes refresh through the parent application.

[BUG] In sharing mode parseRefreshTokenResponse validates against minimumTokenResponseSchema, so accessTokenParsed.data is just {access_token} plus the injected 'refresh_token' placeholder, and the credential.update persists {...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token} — dropping instance_url, id, signature, scope and token_type from the stored key. After the first sharing-mode Salesforce operation the persisted credential key no longer contains instance_url or the other fields jsforce needs; subsequent service instantiations read a stripped key and Salesforce API calls fail.

[BUG] The refreshOAuthTokens contract promises a sync response containing 'only the access token and expiry date', but the Lark path feeds that response into handleLarkError, which validates the Lark {code, msg, data} envelope. With sync enabled the lark refresh response has no code field, so handleLarkError throws on every attempt and Lark Calendar is broken in the feature's primary mode unless the parent endpoint special-cases Lark — contradicting the contract the helper itself documents.

[ADVISORY] The diff introduces an entire new public API route and a shared OAuth-refresh path wired into ten apps with zero tests anywhere in the diff. The exact regression class that shipped here — a safeParse envelope persisted as a credential key, a fetch Response consumed as an axios/gaxios response, a credentialId passed as userId — is what a single unit test per helper would have caught; the next change to this path will be equally blind.

[BUG] The handler never checks req.method and calls appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body) unguarded. Any request that passes the secret check but carries no parseable body (a GET, a content-type mismatch, a malformed payload) throws an unhandled ZodError and returns a 500 instead of a 4xx, so parent-app integration bugs surface as opaque server errors.

[BUG] The decrypted keys blob is JSON.parse'd and written straight into Credential.key with no validation against the target app's credential schema, and the JSON.parse itself is unguarded. A parent app that sends the wrong shape for the app silently poisons the user's stored credential (every subsequent operation for that app fails with nothing surfaced at sync time), and a non-JSON payload throws an unhandled exception returning a 500.

[ADVISORY] The `if (!accessTokenParsed.success) return Promise.reject(...)` branch is unreachable because parseRefreshTokenResponse already throws 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' on !success. The dead branch implies failures are handled gracefully here when they actually throw; the next maintainer editing this flow will reason from a failure-handling path that can never execute.

[ADVISORY] The OAuth redirect URI is rewritten from the config-driven appConfig.slug to the hardcoded string 'zoho-bigin' — a behavior change in a live auth flow traceable to no requirement in a PR about credential sync. An unexplained change to an OAuth redirect flow rides inside a security-sensitive PR, so it cannot be reverted or audited independently of the feature, and any future slug change in config.json now silently desyncs add.ts from the app's own configuration.

[ADVISORY] The secret header is looked up with process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME verbatim, but Node lowercases all incoming request header names. Any operator who sets the env var with an uppercase character (e.g. 'Calcom-Webhook-Secret') makes the lookup undefined and every sync request fail with 403, silently disabling credential sync with no error logged; the only guard is a comment in .env.example.

[ADVISORY] The PR bundles a pure file-relocation refactor — createOAuthAppCredential, encodeOAuthState and decodeOAuthState moved into _utils/oauth/ with import-path churn across ~15 otherwise-untouched app files, including the obtuse self-referencing '../oauth/decodeOAuthState' import from inside the same directory — work not required by the credential-sync feature. Git blame and history for three shared OAuth utilities are severed and the revert surface of a security-sensitive change is inflated; the feature cannot be reverted without also reverting the moves.

[ADVISORY] The webhook secret is compared with a plain !== string comparison. A network-adjacent attacker can attempt byte-by-byte timing recovery of CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET and then overwrite any user's app credentials through this endpoint; crypto.timingSafeEqual closes the oracle.

[BUG] parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the entire zod safeParse result wrapper ({success, data}), but GoogleCalendarService stores that wrapper directly as credential.key where the previous code stored googleCredentialSchema.parse()'s parsed data, so every persisted Google credential key now takes the shape {success:true, data:{...}}. After the first token refresh (Google access tokens expire within ~1 hour of deploy), the stored key no longer has access_token/refresh_token at the top level, so the service constructor's googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key) throws on every subsequent Google Calendar operation: availability checks and booking CRUD return 500 for all Google-connected users, and each user must manually re-authenticate because the old tokens are buried under the wrapper's data with no migration path.

[BUG] The sharing-enabled branch returns the raw fetch Response from CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT without calling response.json(), while every call site consumes the return value as the provider's already-parsed token object (gaxios {res:{data}} for Google, axios {data} for zoho-bigin/zohocrm, the HubSpot SDK token object). With credential sharing enabled, GoogleCalendarService reads res?.data (a fetch Response has no .data) and crashes with TypeError reading 'access_token'; zoho-bigin and zohocrm evaluate tokenInfo.data.error (TypeError on undefined .data); HubspotCalendarService reads .access_token/.expires_in off the Response and persists undefined tokens and a NaN expiry, destroying the working credential — and since one endpoint must simultaneously satisfy Google's .data wrapper, HubSpot's flat token object, and Lark's {code,data} envelope, no single response body can make all wrapped apps work.

[BUG] minimumTokenResponseSchema's two computed keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] both evaluate to the same '[object Object]' string (the second silently overwrites the first), so the intended 'any numeric property is the expiry' rule never exists, zod enforces only access_token and strips every undeclared field (including the refresh_token and expiry the sync contract promises), after which the fallback injects the literal string "refresh_token" as the refresh token. In sharing mode the parsed .data is only {access_token, refresh_token:"refresh_token"}: Office365CalendarService spreads it over o365AuthCredentials and persists it (the real Microsoft refresh_token is overwritten with the literal and expires_in stays stale so every operation re-refreshes), Zoom merges it into the stored key, and SalesforceCalendarService's {...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token} persists {access_token, refresh_token} — dropping instance_url, id, signature, scope and token_type from the stored key — so each affected user's OAuth connection is bricked on the next provider call and the rotated refresh token is unrecoverable without manual re-auth.

[BUG] The sharing branch has no timeout, no error handling, and no fallback to the local refreshFunction when the sync endpoint fails, making the remote parent application a synchronous single point of failure inside the token-refresh path of every calendar and video operation. While CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is unreachable or erroring, every token refresh for sharing-enabled users fails (a rejected fetch or a non-OK Response that downstream parsers throw on), so every booking, availability check, and meeting creation for those users fails — even for providers whose locally stored refresh_token and app keys could have refreshed the token directly via refreshFunction.

[BUG] The zoho-bigin call passes `credentialId` — this class's field holding the credential row's id — as the third userId parameter of refreshOAuthTokens, which every other call site in the diff fills with credential.userId, so the sync request sends calcomUserId=<credential row id>. With sharing enabled, the parent application receives a calcomUserId that is actually the credential row's primary key, resolves the wrong user's token mapping (or none), and zoho-bigin token refresh fails or fetches another user's credentials.

[ADVISORY] SalesforceCalendarService now performs an unconditional OAuth refresh — a POST to login.salesforce.com plus a credential DB write — in its constructor on every instantiation, with no expiry check and, alone among the apps in this PR, without routing through refreshOAuthTokens. Every Salesforce calendar operation (availability checks, booking CRUD) pays a blocking round-trip to Salesforce and hard-fails with HttpError 400 whenever Salesforce is slow or rate-limits, where the previous code reused the stored access token and let jsforce refresh on demand; and when credential sharing is enabled, Salesforce bypasses the parent-app sync endpoint that every other app uses, leaving a parallel refresh path that the sharing architecture does not account for.

[ADVISORY] The webhook payload carries only (userId, appSlug) with no way to address a specific credential, and the handler picks its update target with findFirst over (userId, appId) with no ordering, while Cal.com's data model legitimately allows multiple credentials per user per app (a user with two connected Google accounts). For any multi-credential user the webhook overwrites an arbitrary one of their credentials — whichever row Prisma returns first — so the user's second connected account silently receives the first account's tokens or keeps stale ones, and bookings intermittently create events on the wrong connected account with no error surfaced.

[BUG] The findFirst-then-create sequence is a check-then-insert TOCTOU with no unique constraint backing it (Credential has no unique index on userId+appId; multiple credentials per pair are a supported state), so two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user and app both observe no credential and both take the create branch. A parent-app retry racing the original delivery (classic after a slow first response) leaves the user with duplicate credentials for the app — subsequent pushes update only the first row while the duplicate retains the initial, soon-rotated-out tokens and stays attached to the user, so booking flows that iterate the user's credentials intermittently authenticate with the dead copy and fail.

[ADVISORY] The handler persists the decrypted `keys` JSON into credential.key with no validation against the target app's credential schema (googleCredentialSchema, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema, etc.) and no documented key-shape contract beyond 'Keys should be AES256 encrypted'. Any mismatch between the parent application's payload and the per-app key structure — including drift introduced by a cal.com version upgrade that changes an app's schema — is accepted with a 200 and destructively replaces a working credential with JSON the app's constructor parse rejects, silently bricking every affected user's integration with no error surfaced to either side and no rollback of the overwritten key.

[ADVISORY] The sharing-enabled code paths — the only mode in which this feature operates in production — are unreachable in every CI and test run because APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are env-gated and set nowhere in the repo, and the diff adds no test for the webhook handler or either new util. A green build never executes the changed code that self-hosters actually run: the sharing-branch crashes and credential corruption (the raw Response consumed as a token object, the literal 'refresh_token' sentinel persisted) shipped undetected, and the next regression in these branches will ship the same way.

[BUG] parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the full zod safeParse result ({success, data}) whereas the replaced googleCredentialSchema.parse returned the parsed data, so `key` is the result envelope and is persisted directly via prisma.credential.update({data: {key}}). adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The refreshOAuthTokens contract promises a sync response containing 'only the access token and expiry date', but the Lark path feeds that response into handleLarkError, which validates the Lark {code, msg, data} envelope. With sync enabled the lark refresh response has no code field, so handleLarkError throws on every attempt and Lark Calendar is broken in the feature's primary mode unless the parent endpoint special-cases Lark — contradicting the contract the helper itself documents.

adjudication.rationale: In `refreshOAuthTokens` the sync path calls `fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` and (per its own comment) expects a response that "should only contain the access token and expiry date". But in `packages/app-store/larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the returned `resp` is immediately passed to `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, ...)`, which is a Lark-specific response handler and (by its generic type and typical Lark API patterns) expects the Lark refresh endpoint’s `{ code, msg, data }`-style envelope, not a minimal token payload. Since the sync endpoint is not required (and per comment is discouraged) to return the Lark envelope, enabling `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` + `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` plausibly breaks Lark refreshes unless the external endpoint special-cases Lark to mimic Lark’s response shape—contradicting the helper’s stated contract.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The diff introduces an entire new public API route and a shared OAuth-refresh path wired into ten apps with zero tests anywhere in the diff. The exact regression class that shipped here — a safeParse envelope persisted as a credential key, a fetch Response consumed as an axios/gaxios response, a credentialId passed as userId — is what a single unit test per helper would have caught; the next change to this path will be equally blind.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The handler never checks req.method and calls appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body) unguarded. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The decrypted keys blob is JSON.parse'd and written straight into Credential.key with no validation against the target app's credential schema, and the JSON.parse itself is unguarded. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The OAuth redirect URI is rewritten from the config-driven appConfig.slug to the hardcoded string 'zoho-bigin' — a behavior change in a live auth flow traceable to no requirement in a PR about credential sync. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The secret header is looked up with process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME verbatim, but Node lowercases all incoming request header names. Any operator who sets the env var with an uppercase character (e.g. 'Calcom-Webhook-Secret') makes the lookup undefined and every sync request fail with 403, silently disabling credential sync with no error logged; the only guard is a comment in .env.example.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the secret check indexes `req.headers[...]` using `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` directly: `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]`. In Node/Next, `req.headers` keys are normalized to lowercase, while the env var may contain mixed/uppercase (e.g. `Calcom-Webhook-Secret`). Since the lookup is case-sensitive on the object key, this can evaluate to `undefined` and cause every request to fail the secret comparison, returning 403. The diff only adds a comment in `.env.example` advising lowercase; the code does not enforce/normalize it.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The PR bundles a pure file-relocation refactor — createOAuthAppCredential, encodeOAuthState and decodeOAuthState moved into _utils/oauth/ with import-path churn across ~15 otherwise-untouched app files, including the obtuse self-referencing '../oauth/decodeOAuthState' import from inside the same directory — work not required by the credential-sync feature. The claim that history/blame is 'severed' is less verifiable from the diff alone (git can often follow renames), but the scope/revert-surface concern is concretely grounded in the shown changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The webhook secret is compared with a plain !== string comparison. A network-adjacent attacker can attempt byte-by-byte timing recovery of CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET and then overwrite any user's app credentials through this endpoint; crypto.timingSafeEqual closes the oracle.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added endpoint `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the webhook secret check uses a direct `!==` comparison: `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. This is not a constant-time comparison and can act as a timing oracle for `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. If the secret is recovered, the handler allows updating/creating credentials for an arbitrary `userId` (`prisma.credential.update/create` keyed by `reqBody.userId` + `appSlug`), so an attacker could overwrite users' app credentials via this endpoint.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the entire zod safeParse result wrapper ({success, data}), but GoogleCalendarService stores that wrapper directly as credential.key where the previous code stored googleCredentialSchema.parse()'s parsed data, so every persisted Google credential key now takes the shape {success:true, data:{...}}. After the first token refresh (Google access tokens expire within ~1 hour of deploy), the stored key no longer has access_token/refresh_token at the top level, so the service constructor's googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key) throws on every subsequent Google Calendar operation: availability checks and booking CRUD return 500 for all Google-connected users, and each user must manually re-authenticate because the old tokens are buried under the wrapper's data with no migration path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the Zod `safeParse` result object (it returns `refreshTokenResponse`, not `refreshTokenResponse.data`). In `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the refreshed credential `key` is now set to `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...)` and persisted via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`, which will store `{ success: true, data: ... }` instead of the plain parsed credential object previously produced by `googleCredentialSchema.parse(...)`. This alters the persisted shape of `credential.key` and would break any later code that expects `credential.key` to have `access_token`, `refresh_token`, etc. at the top level.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The sharing-enabled branch returns the raw fetch Response from CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT without calling response.json(), while every call site consumes the return value as the provider's already-parsed token object (gaxios {res:{data}} for Google, axios {data} for zoho-bigin/zohocrm, the HubSpot SDK token object). With credential sharing enabled, GoogleCalendarService reads res?.data (a fetch Response has no .data) and crashes with TypeError reading 'access_token'; zoho-bigin and zohocrm evaluate tokenInfo.data.error (TypeError on undefined .data); HubspotCalendarService reads .access_token/.expires_in off the Response and persists undefined tokens and a NaN expiry, destroying the working credential — and since one endpoint must simultaneously satisfy Google's .data wrapper, HubSpot's flat token object, and Lark's {code,data} envelope, no single response body can make all wrapped apps work.

[BUG] minimumTokenResponseSchema's two computed keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] both evaluate to the same '[object Object]' string (the second silently overwrites the first), so the intended 'any numeric property is the expiry' rule never exists, zod enforces only access_token and strips every undeclared field (including the refresh_token and expiry the sync contract promises), after which the fallback injects the literal string "refresh_token" as the refresh token. In sharing mode the parsed .data is only {access_token, refresh_token:"refresh_token"}: Office365CalendarService spreads it over o365AuthCredentials and persists it (the real Microsoft refresh_token is overwritten with the literal and expires_in stays stale so every operation re-refreshes), Zoom merges it into the stored key, and SalesforceCalendarService's {...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token} persists {access_token, refresh_token} — dropping instance_url, id, signature, scope and token_type from the stored key — so each affected user's OAuth connection is bricked on the next provider call and the rotated refresh token is unrecoverable without manual re-auth.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`, which both evaluate to the same string key (the `toString()` of a Zod object, e.g. `"[object Object]"`), so the second overwrites the first and the intended “any numeric property is expiry” rule is not actually represented. Since `z.object(...)` strips unknown keys by default, in sharing mode (`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`) the safeParse result will keep essentially only `access_token` (and possibly an optional `"[object Object]"` field) while dropping fields like `refresh_token`, `expiry_date`/`expires_in`, `instance_url`, etc. The function then injects a literal `"refresh_token"` string when `refresh_token` is missing. The diff shows callers persisting/merging this parsed data (e.g. Office365 spreads `tokenResponse.data` into `o365AuthCredentials` and updates Prisma; Salesforce updates Prisma with `{...accessTokenParsed.data, refresh_token: credentialKey.refresh_token}`), which can overwrite/lose critical token fields and break future provider calls.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The sharing branch has no timeout, no error handling, and no fallback to the local refreshFunction when the sync endpoint fails, making the remote parent application a synchronous single point of failure inside the token-refresh path of every calendar and video operation. While CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is unreachable or erroring, every token refresh for sharing-enabled users fails (a rejected fetch or a non-OK Response that downstream parsers throw on), so every booking, availability check, and meeting creation for those users fails — even for providers whose locally stored refresh_token and app keys could have refreshed the token directly via refreshFunction.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId` is true, the code unconditionally does a `fetch()` to the remote sync endpoint and returns its `Response` without any `try/catch`, `response.ok` check, timeout/abort, or fallback to `refreshFunction()` on failure. If the endpoint is down/unreachable or returns non-OK, the rejection/invalid response will bubble into the calendar/video refresh paths (e.g., Office365 uses `handleErrorsJson(response)`; Google expects token data immediately), causing token refresh to fail rather than falling back to the local provider refresh flow. This creates a synchronous single point of failure in the token refresh path for sharing-enabled users, exactly as the finding describes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The zoho-bigin call passes `credentialId` — this class's field holding the credential row's id — as the third userId parameter of refreshOAuthTokens, which every other call site in the diff fills with credential.userId, so the sync request sends calcomUserId=<credential row id>. With sharing enabled, the parent application receives a calcomUserId that is actually the credential row's primary key, resolves the wrong user's token mapping (or none), and zoho-bigin token refresh fails or fetches another user's credentials.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the call `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes `credentialId` into `refreshOAuthTokens`' third parameter, which is defined as `userId: number | null` (see `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, where it sends `calcomUserId: userId.toString()`). All other updated call sites pass `credential.userId`. If `credentialId` is indeed the credential row primary key (as its name implies), then with sharing enabled the sync request will send the wrong `calcomUserId`, causing token refresh/mapping failures or mismatches.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] SalesforceCalendarService now performs an unconditional OAuth refresh — a POST to login.salesforce.com plus a credential DB write — in its constructor on every instantiation, with no expiry check and, alone among the apps in this PR, without routing through refreshOAuthTokens. Every Salesforce calendar operation (availability checks, booking CRUD) pays a blocking round-trip to Salesforce and hard-fails with HttpError 400 whenever Salesforce is slow or rate-limits, where the previous code reused the stored access token and let jsforce refresh on demand; and when credential sharing is enabled, Salesforce bypasses the parent-app sync endpoint that every other app uses, leaving a parallel refresh path that the sharing architecture does not account for.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the PR adds an unconditional refresh-token POST to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` followed by a `prisma.credential.update(...)` before returning a `jsforce.Connection`. This has no expiry/need check and is not routed through the new `refreshOAuthTokens(...)` helper used elsewhere in this PR, so when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` + `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set, Salesforce will not follow the same credential-sync path as the other integrations. The diff does not prove this runs “in the constructor on every instantiation” or that prior behavior was jsforce-driven refresh-on-demand, but it does concretely show the new always-refresh + always-write behavior in the connection setup path and the inconsistency with the new sharing architecture.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The webhook payload carries only (userId, appSlug) with no way to address a specific credential, and the handler picks its update target with findFirst over (userId, appId) with no ordering, while Cal.com's data model legitimately allows multiple credentials per user per app (a user with two connected Google accounts). For any multi-credential user the webhook overwrites an arbitrary one of their credentials — whichever row Prisma returns first — so the user's second connected account silently receives the first account's tokens or keeps stale ones, and bookings intermittently create events on the wrong connected account with no error surfaced.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the webhook body schema only includes `{ userId, appSlug, keys }` and the handler locates an existing credential via `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId: reqBody.userId, appId: appMetadata.slug } })` with no ordering. If more than one credential row can exist for the same `(userId, appId)` (which `findFirst` itself implies is possible, and no unique constraint is shown in the diff), the update path will arbitrarily overwrite whichever row Prisma returns first, making the sync non-deterministic for multi-credential users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The findFirst-then-create sequence is a check-then-insert TOCTOU with no unique constraint backing it (Credential has no unique index on userId+appId; multiple credentials per pair are a supported state), so two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user and app both observe no credential and both take the create branch. A parent-app retry racing the original delivery (classic after a slow first response) leaves the user with duplicate credentials for the app — subsequent pushes update only the first row while the duplicate retains the initial, soon-rotated-out tokens and stays attached to the user, so booking flows that iterate the user's credentials intermittently authenticate with the dead copy and fail.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the handler does a `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` and then either `create` or `update`. This check-then-act sequence is not atomic; two concurrent webhook requests for the same `(userId, appSlug)` can both observe no row and both execute the `create` branch, producing duplicate credentials for the same pair. Subsequent webhook deliveries will only update whichever row `findFirst` happens to return, leaving the other duplicate stale.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The handler persists the decrypted `keys` JSON into credential.key with no validation against the target app's credential schema (googleCredentialSchema, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema, etc.) and no documented key-shape contract beyond 'Keys should be AES256 encrypted'. Any mismatch between the parent application's payload and the per-app key structure — including drift introduced by a cal.com version upgrade that changes an app's schema — is accepted with a 200 and destructively replaces a working credential with JSON the app's constructor parse rejects, silently bricking every affected user's integration with no error surfaced to either side and no rollback of the overwritten key.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the decrypted payload is parsed as `const keys = JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` and then written directly to `prisma.credential.update/create({ data: { key: keys, ... } })` with no validation against any per-app credential schema (no zod parse, no shape checks). As a result, any malformed/incorrect key structure sent by the external webhook (including schema drift) will be accepted and will overwrite an existing working credential, potentially breaking integrations later when app code expects a different structure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The sharing-enabled code paths — the only mode in which this feature operates in production — are unreachable in every CI and test run because APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are env-gated and set nowhere in the repo, and the diff adds no test for the webhook handler or either new util. A green build never executes the changed code that self-hosters actually run: the sharing-branch crashes and credential corruption (the raw Response consumed as a token object, the literal 'refresh_token' sentinel persisted) shipped undetected, and the next regression in these branches will ship the same way.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces real, verifiable defects in the env-gated “sharing enabled” paths. `refreshOAuthTokens()` returns a raw `Response` when sharing is enabled (`fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)`), but callers like Google Calendar still treat the return as an axios/gaxios-style object (`const token = res?.data;` in `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`), which will be `undefined` and then crashes on `token.access_token`. Additionally, `parseRefreshTokenResponse()` returns a Zod `safeParse` result object (with `.success`/`.data`), but Google Calendar now persists that whole result to `credential.key` (`data: { key }`), corrupting stored credentials. Separately, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is incorrectly defined with computed keys like `[z.string().toString()]`, which does not implement “any numeric expiry property” and will not validate arbitrary token responses as intended. The finding’s point that CI/tests won’t hit these env-gated branches is consistent with the diff (no tests and new vars only in `.env.example`), but even without that, the functional bugs are directly shown in the changed code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the full zod safeParse result ({success, data}) whereas the replaced googleCredentialSchema.parse returned the parsed data, so `key` is the result envelope and is persisted directly via prisma.credential.update({data: {key}}). In the default sharing-disabled configuration, the first Google token refresh rewrites the stored credential key to {success:true, data:{...}}; the next operation reads that malformed key and every subsequent Google Calendar call (availability, booking) fails until the user reinstalls the app — silent credential corruption for all Google users of any deployment.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, the function returns the Zod `safeParse` result object (`{ success, data, error }`) after throwing on `!success`, not the parsed `data` itself. In `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the prior `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` (which returns the parsed value) was replaced with `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` and then persisted via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. This will store the safeParse envelope into the credential `key` field rather than the credential payload, corrupting stored credentials in the non-sharing path (where `schema.safeParse` is used). The diff also shows other call sites (e.g. Office365) treating the return value as a safeParse result (`tokenResponse.success` / `tokenResponse.data`), confirming the mismatch in Google’s usage.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] With credential sharing enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the sync endpoint's raw fetch Response, but the code reads res?.data which is undefined on a Response, so token.access_token on the next line throws a TypeError before anything is updated. Every Google Calendar operation fails with an unhandled TypeError (reading 'access_token') in any deployment with APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT set.

adjudication.rationale: In the new `refreshOAuthTokens` helper, when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId`, it does `const response = await fetch(...); return response;` (i.e., a raw `Response`). But in `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the refresh path does `const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...); const token = res?.data; googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token;`, which assumes an axios/gaxios-like object with a `.data` field. A Fetch `Response` has no `.data`, so `token` becomes `undefined` and `token.access_token` will throw a `TypeError`. This is directly verifiable from the diff and would break Google Calendar token refresh when the sync endpoint is enabled.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The documented sync contract ("The response should only contain the access token and expiry date") is returned as a bare fetch Response to nine call sites that each expect a vendor-specific object (google-auth result with .res.data, a HubspotToken, a Lark {code,msg,data} envelope, axios results with .data), so no caller can consume the delegated response as documented. Self-hosters who enable credential sharing get TypeErrors or corrupted credentials on every delegated refresh across google-calendar, hubspot, lark-calendar, office365calendar, office365video, webex, zoomvideo, zohocrm and zoho-bigin — the feature's happy path works for no app.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, when credential sharing is enabled it does `fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` and returns the *raw* `Response`. Multiple call sites treat the return value as a vendor/SDK/axios-shaped object, not a `Response`: e.g. Google Calendar does `const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...); const token = res?.data;` (but `Response` has no `.data`), Hubspot assigns it to `HubspotToken` (but gets `Response`), and Zoho (bigin/zohocrm) wraps axios refreshes but would receive a `Response` and then access `.data` (TypeError). This mismatch means enabling the feature will break delegated refresh flows at least in these paths, consistent with the finding’s claim that the documented contract is not consumable by callers as implemented.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] In sharing mode the fetch Response assigned to hubspotRefreshToken: HubspotToken carries none of the token fields, so the expiry computation that follows the call ("set expiry date as offset from current time" using expires_in) produces NaN and the access token read is undefined. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] refreshOAuthTokens is passed `credentialId` — the credential's primary key — as the userId argument, so sharing-mode zoho-bigin refresh posts `calcomUserId=<credentialId>` to the sync endpoint instead of the user's ID, and the returned fetch Response (no axios-style `.data`) makes `tokenInfo.data.error` throw a TypeError on line 96 anyway. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] In sharing mode the fetch Response returned by refreshOAuthTokens is treated as a HubspotToken: `hubspotRefreshToken.expires_in` is undefined so the computed expiry_date becomes NaN, and the Response object itself is what the subsequent credential update persists (a fetch Response serializes to an empty object in the Json column). adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, when sharing mode is enabled (`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId`), the function returns the raw `fetch(...)` result (a `Response`). adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The sync webhook writes the decrypted payload straight into credential.key with no validation against the app's credential schema, no preservation of the previous key, and an unhandled JSON.parse around the decrypted string. A sync endpoint bug (wrong app's keys, partial payload, plaintext instead of ciphertext) silently overwrites user credentials with garbage and returns a 500 — the damage surfaces only when bookings fail and the previous key is already gone; this writer bypasses the zod guards every other credential write path applies.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the handler decrypts and `JSON.parse`s `reqBody.keys` (`const keys = JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))`) without any try/catch, so malformed ciphertext/plaintext or non-JSON will throw and yield a 500. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] In sharing mode zohoCrmTokenInfo is a fetch Response with no `.data` property (that is an axios-response field), so `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` throws a TypeError on every zohocrm token refresh. With sharing enabled, zohocrm credentials are never refreshed through the sync endpoint; bookings fail once the stored access token expires, and the parent app's tokens are never used for this app despite it being routed through the sync path.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the token refresh call is wrapped in `refreshOAuthTokens(...)`. When sharing is enabled (`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` and `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` and `credential.userId` truthy), `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a `fetch` `Response` object (see `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`). adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] In sharing mode `resp` is the sync endpoint's Response, but handleLarkError json-parses it and throws whenever `data.code !== 0`, and the documented sync payload ({access_token, expiry}) has no `code` field. adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the refresh flow now always passes `resp` into `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, this.log)`. But `resp` can come from `refreshOAuthTokens()`, which in sharing mode (`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId`) calls `fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` and returns that Response. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Both computed keys in minimumTokenResponseSchema stringify to the literal property name "[object Object]" (ZodString has no toString override), so the second silently overwrites the first and the schema degenerates to `{access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown-optional}` — the intended "any numeric property is the expiry" validation never exists. In sharing mode, token payloads with no expiry or numeric field at all pass validation and are persisted into credential.key, so downstream expiry logic receives undefined/NaN (tokens re-refreshed per call or mis-stored) and no error is raised at sync time to warn the operator.

As a result, the schema does not enforce “any numeric property is the expiry” as intended and can accept responses lacking any numeric expiry field when `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is active.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The Salesforce service now performs an unconditional OAuth refresh — a blocking POST to login.salesforce.com plus a prisma.credential.update — inside the constructor promise, before any API call, with no check of whether the stored access token is still valid. Cal.com instantiates calendar services per request (availability checks on booking page views and every booking operation), so each view by a user with Salesforce installed now makes a blocking Salesforce OAuth round-trip and a credential DB write; a Salesforce outage or OAuth rate-limit fails all those operations even while the stored access token was still valid, and page-view-frequency refreshes hammer the token endpoint.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the service now does a token refresh unconditionally during connection initialization: it immediately `fetch`es `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` using the stored `refresh_token`, throws on non-OK, then does `prisma.credential.update(...)` before returning `new jsforce.Connection(...)`. There is no check of access-token validity/expiry before forcing this refresh, so any Salesforce token endpoint outage/rate-limit or transient failure will now break service instantiation even if the existing stored access token would have worked, and it also adds an avoidable DB write on each instantiation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The lax-schema branch gates only on APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, without the `userId` condition that refreshOAuthTokens applies, so token responses fetched from the real provider — team credentials (userId null, which createOAuthAppCredential in this diff explicitly supports) and Salesforce, which never routes through the sync endpoint — are parsed with the stripping minimum schema. For a team-level installed credential on a sharing-enabled deployment, the real provider refresh response is stripped to `{access_token}` and the injected placeholder overwrites the working refresh_token in the persisted credential; the next refresh sends refresh_token='refresh_token', the provider rejects it, and the team's integration is silently bricked.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, routing to the sync endpoint is gated by `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId` (requires a user credential). However `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts` switches to the lax `minimumTokenResponseSchema` on only `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, with no `userId`/“was synced” condition. Because Zod objects strip unknown keys by default, this minimum schema will drop provider-returned fields like `refresh_token` when the refresh actually came from the real provider (e.g., team credentials where `credential.userId` is null so `refreshOAuthTokens` calls the provider, not the sync endpoint). Then `parseRefreshTokenResponse` injects a placeholder `refresh_token = "refresh_token"`, and consumers like `office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts` merge `tokenResponse.data` back into `o365AuthCredentials`, which would overwrite a real refresh token before persisting the credential. This mismatch is directly visible in the diff and can brick future refreshes for non-user credentials on sharing-enabled deployments.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Both computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` evaluate to the literal string '[object Object]' (Zod schemas do not override Object.prototype.toString), and z.object strips unknown keys, so minimumTokenResponseSchema requires only access_token and discards every other field — the 'assume any property with a number is the expiry' and 'allow other properties' comments describe validation that does not exist. Under sharing, every parsed token response is reduced to `{access_token, refresh_token:'refresh_token'}` regardless of what the endpoint returned: expiry fields never survive, so callers like zoom compute expiryDate from the stripped expires_in (NaN, persisted as null, forcing a refresh on every API call) and salesforce persists a key missing instance_url (reported separately).

These evaluate to a literal string key (e.g. "[object Object]") rather than creating a dynamic key pattern, so the schema effectively only validates `access_token` (and possibly an optional "[object Object]" field) and, because `z.object(...)` strips unknown keys by default, it discards fields like `expires_in`/`expiry_date`, `instance_url`, etc. Under `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`, callers that previously relied on those fields (e.g. Zoom/Office365 parsing and Salesforce persisting `instance_url`) will lose them, leading to incorrect expiry handling and incomplete credential data.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The findFirst-then-update/create sequence has no in-flight guard and no unique constraint on (userId, appId), so concurrent deliveries for the same user+app race. Overlapping deliveries (caller retries or parallel syncs) both find no credential and both create, leaving duplicate credential rows; later syncs update an arbitrary row and the stale duplicates cause intermittent auth failures that flip depending on which row the credential loader picks.

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the handler does a non-atomic `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` followed by either `credential.update` or `credential.create`. There is no transaction/locking or `upsert` here, so concurrent webhook deliveries for the same `(userId, appSlug)` could race and both take the create path unless the database enforces a unique constraint. The finding’s specific claim that there is *no* unique constraint on `(userId, appId)` is not verifiable from this diff (schema not shown), but the code pattern is still a concrete concurrency risk introduced by the new endpoint.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the secret check indexes `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]`.
